title: Still on Stage
subject: English
unit: Spring 2: The Tempest (Shakespeare): transformation through forgiveness
source: Written for english/y7 lesson 25 ('Still on Stage' (teacher-written information article, pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 25: Non-fiction: why is Shakespeare still studied?. Read the whole text, then annotate it: underline the writer's methods and note their effect in the margin.

passage.title: Still on Stage
paras: Every year, millions of students open a play written four centuries ago. Why? Partly because Shakespeare shaped the language we speak: phrases such as 'break the ice' and 'wild-goose chase' first appear in his plays. Partly because his stories travel: his plays have been translated into more than a hundred languages and turned into films, novels and cartoons. But mostly, it is because he understood people. Jealousy, ambition, grief and forgiveness have not changed since 1611. Reading Shakespeare is not a history lesson; it is a mirror.

Some readers find his language hard at first, and that is understandable. Words change over time, and a joke that made a crowd laugh in London in 1611 may need a footnote today. Yet the difficulty is part of the reward. When a line finally makes sense, readers feel they have earned it.

His plays were also written to be performed, not only read. Shakespeare wrote for an open-air theatre where the audience stood close to the stage, ate, talked and shouted back at the actors. Seeing a scene acted out often makes the meaning suddenly clear.

Finally, his characters are rarely simple heroes or villains. Prospero, in The Tempest, is wronged, but he is also controlling; he chooses mercy, but only after he has the power to punish. Students argue about him, and that argument is exactly the point. A good story does not tell us what to think. It makes us think.
Four hundred years on, the curtain has not come down. As long as people are jealous, ambitious, grieving and able to forgive, Shakespeare will still be on stage.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
questions.a: Shakespeare is still worth studying because he understood people: his themes have not changed.

questions.q: Find two methods the writer uses and explain the effect of each.
questions.a: Rhetorical question ('Why?') draws the reader in; examples of phrases ('break the ice'); the metaphor 'it is a mirror'; the list of emotions.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph end the argument?
questions.a: It returns to the stage image ('the curtain has not come down'), giving a confident, circular conclusion.

questions.q: Retrieve four facts from the article.
questions.a: Any four: millions study him; 'break the ice' and 'wild-goose chase' first appear in his plays; translated into over 100 languages; adapted into films, novels and cartoons; The Tempest dates from 1611.

questions.q: What does the metaphor 'it is a mirror' suggest?
questions.a: That reading Shakespeare shows us ourselves: our own feelings and behaviour.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, explain the writer's viewpoint and two methods used to persuade. Starter: 'The writer believes that... One method is...'
questions.a: The writer believes Shakespeare is still relevant; methods such as facts (100 languages) and the closing metaphor, each with an effect.

questions.q: Extend: link the article to The Tempest: which 'unchanged' feeling does the play explore?
Stretch: is the article convincing? Give one reason for and one against.
questions.a: For: facts and examples. Against: it gives no other side, e.g. reasons to read newer writers.

questions.q: What is the writer's main viewpoint?
options: Shakespeare is still worth reading because he understood people
Shakespeare is too old for schools
questions.a: A) Shakespeare is still worth reading because he understood people. The final sentences give the main view; B is the opposite; C is never said.

questions.q: 'Translated into more than a hundred languages' is a...
Answer the ponder in one sentence, using one idea from the article.
questions.a: For example: schools should still teach him because his plays show feelings that have not changed since 1611.
